result: The visual system contextualizes incomplete scene fragments by exploiting spatial schemata, with schema-based sorting occurring specifically in the occipital place area (OPA) and within the first 200 ms of vision. This sorting is based on the fragments' vertical location within the scene schema, with vertical location predicting neural representations in OPA (t[29]=4.12, p<0.001) but not in V1 or PPA, and predicting EEG responses between 55-685 ms (peak t[19]=9.03, p<0.001) with consistent peaks around 200 ms across all analyses.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C27-C29, and C47-C49 provide converging spatiotemporal evidence from both fMRI and EEG data with appropriate statistical testing and multiple comparison corrections. The specificity to OPA (not V1 or PPA) and the consistent temporal profile around 200 ms across analyses strengthen the conclusion. The experimental design appropriately controls for explicit location cues by presenting all fragments at central fixation.

result: Schema-based coding operates flexibly across visual features as measured by deep neural network models. After removing DNN features (ResNet50 and AlexNet), category information was abolished in both fMRI and EEG signals, but vertical location information persisted in OPA (t[29]=2.37, p=0.012) and in EEG responses (75-335 ms, peak t[19]=5.06, p<0.001), demonstrating that schematic coding cannot be explained by categorization-related features extracted by current DNN models.
evaluation: Claims C4, C36-C40, C68-C70, and C86-C88 demonstrate that the schema effect persists after controlling for DNN features, with appropriate statistical tests showing significant effects. The use of two different DNN architectures (ResNet50 and AlexNet) with similar results strengthens the conclusion. The successful removal of category information validates the DNN control approach, while the persistence of vertical location information supports the flexibility claim.

result: Schema-based coding operates flexibly across different types of environments (indoor and outdoor scenes). When analyses were restricted to comparisons between indoor and outdoor scenes, vertical location still predicted cortical organization in OPA (t[29]=3.05, p=0.002) and EEG responses (70-385 ms, peak t[19]=7.47, p<0.001), indicating that schematic coding generalizes across radically different scene types.
evaluation: Claims C5 and C41-C43 demonstrate generalization across scene categories with appropriate statistical testing. The cross-category analysis is a strong test of flexibility since indoor and outdoor scenes differ substantially in visual characteristics. The persistence of vertical location effects when within-category comparisons are excluded supports the claim of flexible operation across environments.

result: After removing both DNN features and within-category comparisons (the most stringent control), vertical location still predicted OPA representations (t[29]=2.38, p=0.012) and EEG responses after 180 ms (peak t[19]=4.41, p<0.001), with early schema effects rendered non-significant. This temporal pattern suggests a high degree of flexibility in schematic coding emerging after 180 ms.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 show that schema effects persist under the most stringent control conditions, though with altered temporal dynamics. The delayed onset in EEG (after 180 ms vs. earlier effects in less stringent analyses) is appropriately interpreted as reflecting increased flexibility. The statistical tests are appropriate and the interpretation is consistent with the data pattern.

result: No effects were observed for horizontal location in either fMRI or EEG data, which is consistent with more rigid spatial scene structure in the vertical dimension where the sky is almost always above the ground.
evaluation: Claims C30-C31 report a negative finding that is theoretically motivated and consistent with prior work (Mandler and Parker, 1976). The absence of horizontal location effects contrasts with robust vertical location effects, supporting the hypothesis that schema-based coding follows the more rigid vertical structure of natural scenes. This selective effect strengthens the overall interpretation.

result: Scene category was accurately predicted in both OPA (t[29]=3.12, p=0.002) and PPA (t[29]=4.26, p<0.001) in fMRI data, and from 60-775 ms (peak t[19]=6.39, p<0.001) in EEG data, consistent with previous findings on scene categorization in these regions.
evaluation: Claims C32-C34 demonstrate expected category effects in scene-selective regions with appropriate statistical testing. These findings replicate prior work (Lowe et al., 2018; Walther et al., 2009) and serve as a positive control, validating the experimental approach and analysis methods. The category effects provide important context for interpreting the novel schema-based coding effects.

result: The absence of vertical location effects in V1 and the failure of low-level control models (pixel dissimilarity, GIST, V1 neural dissimilarity) to account for vertical location organization demonstrate that schematic coding is not tied to simple visual features or low-level feature processing.
evaluation: Claims C35 and C90-C93 provide converging evidence from multiple control analyses that low-level features cannot explain the schema effects. The use of V1 neural dissimilarity as a brain-derived control is particularly strong, as it provides an empirical measure of low-level features. The negative findings in V1 and with low-level models, contrasted with positive findings in OPA, support the interpretation that schematic coding reflects higher-level processing.

result: The vertical location organization in neural data reflects prior schematic knowledge about scene structure rather than learning during the experiment, as vertical location effects were present in both the first half (t[29]=3.46, p<0.001) and second half of the experiment with no significant differences between halves.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80 address an important alternative explanation through a split-half analysis. The presence of effects in the first half of the experiment and the absence of differences between halves support the interpretation that effects reflect pre-existing schematic knowledge rather than within-experiment learning. This control strengthens the main interpretation.

result: Schematic coding can be observed consistently across different pairwise comparisons along the vertical axis (top vs. bottom, top vs. middle, middle vs. bottom), although comparisons including the top fragments yielded stronger effects.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 demonstrate that the vertical location effect is not driven by a single pairwise comparison but is present across all vertical comparisons. The stronger effects for comparisons including top fragments is consistent with the sky being a particularly distinctive scene element. This analysis provides additional detail about the nature of the schematic organization.

result: Differences in task difficulty across fragments (measured by accuracy and response time in the indoor/outdoor categorization task) were not related to the neural effects of interest, and schematic coding effects emerging around 200 ms cannot be explained by differences in task difficulty.
evaluation: Claims C74 and C83 address a potential confound through control analyses shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8. The lack of correlation between task difficulty measures and vertical location effects, and the temporal dissociation (task effects late, schema effects at 200 ms), rule out task difficulty as an explanation for the main findings.

result: In EEG data, a categorical predictor for vertical location revealed significantly stronger information from 75-340 ms compared to a Euclidean distance predictor, suggesting that the differentiation along the vertical axis is more categorical in nature.
evaluation: Claims C84-C85 compare two alternative models of vertical location coding and find evidence for categorical rather than graded representation. The statistical comparison between predictors is appropriate, though the finding is specific to EEG data (no difference in fMRI). This provides additional characterization of the nature of schematic coding.

result: The experimental design used six natural scenes (three indoor, three outdoor) split into six fragments each (3 vertical × 2 horizontal), presented at central fixation to remove explicit location information. Thirty participants completed the fMRI experiment and twenty completed the EEG experiment, performing an indoor/outdoor categorization task with high accuracy (fMRI: 94%, EEG: 96%).
evaluation: Claims C21-C26 and C73 describe the experimental design and behavioral performance. The design is appropriate for testing the hypothesis, with adequate sample sizes (n=30 fMRI, n=20 EEG) and good task performance indicating participant engagement. The central presentation of fragments is a key design feature that removes explicit location cues, allowing isolation of schema-based effects.

result: Multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) of neural similarity in OPA and after 200 ms of processing revealed a sorting according to vertical location visible in a two-dimensional solution, with a division into three vertical locations observable around 200 ms, suggesting that schemata are a prominent organizing principle for representations in OPA and after 200 ms of vision.
evaluation: Claims C75-C78 describe visualization analyses (MDS) that complement the main statistical analyses. The MDS provides an intuitive illustration of the schema-based organization and is consistent with the regression-based findings. While visualization is useful for interpretation, the main support comes from the statistical analyses in the primary results.

result: The manuscript provides historical and theoretical context for scene schemata, citing their philosophical origins (Kant, 1781), adaptation by psychology (Barlett, 1932; Piaget, 1926), and their role in representing knowledge about typical scene composition. Prior research demonstrates that scene schemata benefit memory performance and perceptual tasks, with effects more robust along the vertical dimension where scene structure is more rigid.
evaluation: Claims C6-C14 and C17-C20 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the theoretical foundation for the study and are consistent with established knowledge in the field. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

result: The study tests the novel hypothesis that scene schemata support the contextualization of fragmented sensory inputs, predicting that if sensory inputs are processed in relation to schema context, scene fragments from similar typical positions should be processed similarly.
evaluation: Claims C15-C16 state the main hypothesis of the study, which is clearly articulated and logically leads to testable predictions. The hypothesis is novel and well-motivated by prior work. The experimental results (C1-C5, C27-C29, etc.) provide strong support for this hypothesis.

result: The findings characterize a novel neural mechanism for contextualizing fragmented inputs during naturalistic vision, where the mechanism exploits schemata to sort sensory inputs into meaningful representations of the environment, operating during perceptual scene analysis in OPA within the first 200 ms and flexibly across changes in visual properties.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 summarize the main contribution of the study. These summary claims are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple analyses (C1-C5, C27-C29, C36-C46) demonstrating spatiotemporal localization, flexibility across visual features, and generalization across scene types. The characterization as a 'novel mechanism' is justified by the new findings.

result: Schema-based coding in OPA is consistent with the region's important role in visual scene processing, with prior TMS studies showing OPA is crucial for scene discrimination, navigation, and anticipating scene information, and fMRI studies showing OPA computations include spatial layout analysis and parsing of local scene elements.
evaluation: Claims C53-C58 connect the current findings to prior knowledge about OPA function, supported by appropriate citations. The interpretation that schema-based coding fits with OPA's known roles is reasonable, though the claims acknowledge that future studies are needed to clarify which specific computations mediate the observed effects.

result: The study acknowledges limitation to a small set of scenes and speculates that schema-based coding may constitute a more general coding strategy that could generalize to other visual contents (such as faces) and non-visual domains, where the brain may use schematic information to contextualize fragmented and unreliable sensory inputs.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 appropriately acknowledge a limitation (small stimulus set) and offer speculative extensions. C59 is a factual limitation. C60-C61 are explicitly speculative claims about potential generalization that require future empirical testing. The speculation is reasonable but currently unsupported by data in the manuscript.

result: The findings are interpreted as consistent with Bayesian theories of perception where prior information becomes more important with noisy/ambiguous sensory input, and as providing a mechanism for efficient communication between perceptual and cognitive systems by formatting scene information according to its environmental role for efficient readout by downstream processes.
evaluation: Claims C62-C66 offer theoretical interpretations connecting the findings to broader frameworks (Bayesian perception, functional interactions with environment). While these interpretations are plausible and supported by citations to relevant theories, they remain speculative regarding the specific functional role of the observed schema-based coding. The claims are reasonable interpretations but go beyond what the data directly demonstrate.

result: The schema-based sorting of scene information happens during early scene analysis (around 200 ms), making this information accessible to many high-level processes and potentially contributing to optimal use of perceptual information for guiding efficient real-world behaviors even when sensory inputs are incomplete or dynamically changing.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C72 draw functional implications from the temporal findings. The early timing (200 ms) is well-established by the data (C3, C29, C48), supporting the claim about accessibility to downstream processes. The speculation about functional benefits for real-world behavior is reasonable given the early timing and flexibility findings, though direct evidence for behavioral benefits is not provided.

result: The manuscript speculates that augmenting DNN training procedures with schematic information may improve their performance on real-world tasks and narrow the gap between artificial and biological neural networks.
evaluation: Claim C71 is explicitly speculative about future directions for computational modeling, with a citation to Katti et al. (2019). While the suggestion is reasonable given that current DNNs don't capture schema-based organization (C69-C70), this remains an untested prediction about future work rather than a supported finding.

result: GLMs based on ResNet50 RDMs had better fit than those based on AlexNet RDMs, though ResNet50 models had more predictor variables which may contribute to their better fit.
evaluation: Claim C89 reports a comparison between two DNN architectures with appropriate acknowledgment of a confound (different numbers of predictors). The finding is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The caveat about predictor number is appropriate, and the similar qualitative results from both architectures (C88) support the main conclusions regardless of this difference.
